cards.title: Retail arbitrage prep: seller account + scanning app
cards.summary: Set up an Amazon seller account and the Amazon Seller app before sourcing so you can scan barcodes in-store and see live price, fees and gating.
cards.use_when: Product selection for a new or cash-constrained store: you want fast-turn inventory to flip on Amazon with minimal upfront capital.
steps: Sign up for an Amazon seller account first — it is not needed to research products but is required to list and sell. Follow a current walkthrough so you avoid verification problems (interface changes; verify in Seller Central).
Download the Amazon Seller app and log in. Scanning a barcode shows the current Amazon selling price, whether the item is gated, and the estimated Amazon/FBA fees.

For each scan, compare the store price plus inbound shipping to Amazon against the Amazon sell price minus FBA fees. If the buy cost plus your cost to send it in plus Amazon's ship-to-customer fee is not below the sale price, skip the item.
Optionally add a keyword/volume tool so you can check monthly unit sales, i.e. whether anyone is actually buying the item on Amazon before you commit.
Decide your channel: in-store clearance (retail arbitrage), or buying discounted from other websites and shipping in (online arbitrage). Both follow the same buy-low/sell-high logic.
caveats: Retail arbitrage means selling someone else's branded product, so you compete on price for the Buy Box rather than owning a brand asset.
The presenter's income figures are personal results, not benchmarks.
Tool interfaces and fee names change — verify current screens and fees.

cards.title: Reading the Buy Box win rules
cards.summary: The lowest price wins the Buy Box roughly 90% of the time; seller feedback is the secondary factor, so arbitrage pricing must be actively managed.
cards.use_when: Pricing an arbitrage or reseller listing where multiple sellers offer the identical product and you need to know how orders are actually allocated.
steps: Understand the mechanic: customers mostly buy through the main Buy Box; offers not holding the box sit further down the page and get a small fraction of orders (the presenter puts that at under 10%).
To take the box on an existing listing, price at or slightly below the current best offer — a cent or two under is enough per the presenter.

Before undercutting, check how many units are selling per month and how many competing sellers exist. If volume is high relative to the number of sellers, there are enough sales to go around and a short-lived price war matters less.
Watch competitor stock levels. If the current box holder has only a few units left, you can hold a higher price or match theirs and simply outlast them rather than racing to the bottom.
Check listings at minimum daily. Competitors can respond by cutting price, and you may also be able to raise price when rivals sell out.
If you scale past a handful of SKUs, automating repricing frees the time this manual checking consumes — the presenter treats this as optional for beginners on a small budget.
caveats: Seller feedback matters too: if feedback falls too low you can lose orders and lose the box even with the best price, so price alone is not sufficient.
Price-war outcomes are situational; the source presents lowest-price-wins as the dominant but not exclusive rule.

cards.title: Finding arbitrage deals in-store and online
cards.summary: Source clearance and discounted multi-packs where the Amazon 90-day median price is roughly double your buy cost after fees, favouring light non-bulky ungated items.
cards.use_when: Sourcing products for an Amazon reseller operation, whether walking a store or scanning deal pages from your desk.
steps: In store, scour clearance sections and endcaps; online, go to retailer clearance/deal and weekly-ad pages (the walkthrough uses Target deals and Big Lots weekly ad/closeouts).
Filter for small, light, non-bulky items — the presenter avoids furniture because shipping cost destroys the margin. Seasonal decor can work if you accept a limited selling window.
Scan or look up the item on Amazon. Compare against the typical/median price (the 90-day median is used in the example), not just the current buy price, because a spiking low price can be temporary.
Confirm the listing is ungated. Gated products require brand approval, which is not always granted — wait for approval before purchasing the stock.

Estimate total landed cost: purchase price + inbound shipping + FBA/fulfilment fees. In the worked example, a $9.97 puzzle selling around $20-25 showed roughly $7 per unit of room before shipping, still profitable.
Check demand, not just margin. The example item showed ~21 sales/month, which the presenter accepted only because the competing seller had just three units left.
Prefer a source with a local pickup so you collect and ship yourself, avoiding being charged twice for shipping.
caveats: Paid deal-alert groups exist (Telegram/Discord); the presenter warns many are inaccurate or overpriced and suggests not paying more than around $100, with decent groups near $15-20/month — and says they are not necessary.
Online-arbitrage margin can be erased by ignored dimensional weight and shipping; always run the fee calculator.

cards.title: Pricing and prep when listing arbitrage inventory
cards.summary: List scanned inventory as FBA, match barcodes, declare battery/dangerous-goods details, and set prices with min/max so automated repricing protects the Buy Box.
cards.use_when: Listing arbitrage stock and managing prices on Amazon once units are in your hands or sent to FBA.
steps: Confirm the product matches the Amazon listing: check the UPC and, where UPC does not line up, the model number. Listing under a mismatched identifier causes problems later.

Know barcode rules: consumables and cosmetic products generally require an Amazon FNSKU label over the manufacturer barcode; for general goods you can often use the manufacturer barcode. Check the current rule for your category before shipping.
When creating the listing, set condition (e.g. New), quantity, your SKU, and price; then select FBA so Amazon handles pick, pack and ship.
Answer prep and dangerous-goods questions accurately — e.g. the flashlight/battery example declares alkaline AAA batteries packed with the product and not treated as dangerous goods.
Enter box dimensions and weight; if the app throws a size mismatch warning you can confirm and continue when you are confident in the real measurement.
Pack to prevent damage in transit (the walkthrough adds bubble wrap) — damaged-at-Amazon units can be claimed, but poorly prepped units create avoidable problems.

Set a minimum and maximum price per SKU. When no competitor is present, sell at your maximum; when a competitor appears, your price drops automatically toward theirs but never below your floor. Use Reprice to reclaim the Buy Box faster.
caveats: Barcode, prep and hazardous-goods requirements vary by category and can change; verify in Seller Central before each shipment.
Low-quantity launch prices left money on the table in the walkthrough — watch the listing as soon as it goes live to catch early velocity.

cards.title: Managing seller feedback and product-review mix-ups
cards.summary: Monitor seller feedback, challenge misplaced negative product reviews within 30 days, and protect feedback by shipping accurate, undamaged items.
cards.use_when: Running ongoing account health on an FBA or arbitrage store where seller feedback affects Buy Box eligibility and order volume.
steps: Open Feedback Manager regularly to read new ratings; feedback reflects the fulfilment experience, while product reviews reflect the product itself.

Look for product reviews mistakenly left as seller feedback. In the walkthrough a two-star note about receiving only one of two items was removed immediately on request because Amazon fulfilled the order.
Request removal within 30 days — after that the review becomes permanent. Verbatim: 'you can challenge it, but you'll have to do this within the first 30 days'.
For legitimate negative seller feedback, either accept it if positive feedback outweighs it, or contact the buyer through Amazon's buyer-messaging tools.
If you want a negative review reconsidered, offer a refund through proper channels rather than asking directly for the review's removal, which you cannot do explicitly.

Prevent the problem upstream: list the accurate item, package so goods do not arrive damaged, and note that damage occurring after Amazon receives the goods is Amazon's responsibility and can be compensated.
Also monitor your listings for Buy Box position on at least a daily basis, since feedback loss and price loss compound each other.
caveats: The walkthrough's instant removal is Amazon's decision in that case, not a guarantee; outcomes depend on whether Amazon identifies the issue as fulfilment-related.
Never instruct buyers to leave fabricated or traded reviews — the source only discusses refunds and proper messaging.

cards.title: Restocking signals for arbitrage inventory
cards.summary: Amazon indicates restock timing and fast-selling SKUs tell you when to reorder from a store or website while the deal is still live.
cards.use_when: Replenishment decisions for limited-time or seasonal arbitrage products so you do not sit on stock or miss sellable windows.
steps: Track sell-through on the inventory screen to see how fast each SKU moves and where Amazon flags a good restock time.
Recognise that sourcing deals are usually limited-time offers; clearance and weekly-ad pricing will not be available indefinitely.
When a SKU sells out, treat that as two signals: (a) you likely under-priced it, and (b) it may be worth returning to the store or site for a larger quantity if the item is still findable.

Size the reorder against observed monthly velocity — with 100 sales/month and no aggressive competition, the walkthrough judged 15 units could clear within a month — not against how much cash you want to deploy.
Support this with min/max price automation so a high-velocity SKU keeps winning the Buy Box without manual checks while you hunt replacements.
Repeat the loop: keep finding new products, keep expanding SKU count, and remain passive on listings except for price and feedback.
caveats: This supply is opportunistic: if the discounted source dries up, you cannot reliably replenish the same SKU, so do not build retention-dependent promises on it.
The size example is the presenter's reasoning, not a validated sell-through formula.

cards.title: Private-label start-up cost breakdown
cards.summary: A worked private-label launch cost roughly $2,150 before sales: research tool, design, barcodes, seller account, samples, manufacturing and freight.
cards.use_when: Pricing out a first private-label product launch and deciding how much cash the business needs before the first sale.
steps: Budget the pre-launch stack from the walkthrough: ~$130 research tool for the first month, ~$200 packaging design on Fiverr, ~$120 for four GS1 UPC codes, ~$39.99 Amazon seller account, ~$200 manufacturer samples via Alibaba, ~$1,192 manufacturing, ~$145 sea freight.
Do manufacturing before freight and confirm landed unit cost across the full order — the presenter's core error was ordering inventory without running the profit math first.

Consider the legal layer separately: an LLC (roughly $200 via a registered agent) separates personal and business assets if you are sued; a DBA (about $99) gives a trading name but no liability protection; a USPTO trademark is roughly $250-275 and can be self-filed.
Use GS1 codes rather than resold barcodes; a single UPC runs around $30 but multi-SKU product lines multiply the cost.
Weigh sea versus air freight: sea is cheaper but much slower, so factor the cash-flow gap into launch timing.
Recruit design help if needed — logo designer, packaging designer and listing photography are three separate jobs; the walkthrough got photography free from a friend.
caveats: All figures are one seller's 2020s-era costs and will vary by product, supplier and freight market; treat them as a planning shape, not a quote.
Cheap multi-SKU launches raise total cost and complexity before you know what sells.

cards.title: Month-by-month P&L and the referral/FBA/PPC fee structure
cards.summary: Every dollar of revenue is reduced by a roughly 15% referral fee, FBA pick-pack-ship fees and PPC spend, so read revenue as gross and track net profit per month.
cards.use_when: Financial planning and pricing decisions on an Amazon store, and judging whether a listing is genuinely profitable after fees and ads.
steps: Separate revenue from profit explicitly. The walkthrough's first 30 days: $173 revenue from 39 units, ~$285 production cost, ~$130 referral fee (about 15%), ~$170 FBA fee, ~$100 PPC — landing at roughly $186 net in his accounting.
Track the three main deductions every month: referral fee (a percentage of sale price), FBA fulfilment fee (pick, pack, ship), and advertising spend.
Model month two scale-up to see fixed vs variable cost behaviour: $1,800 revenue on 82 units produced $385 net after $599 production, $272 referral, $357 FBA and $200 PPC.
Expect volatile months: later months included a small loss and very small profits before recovering, so do not judge the business on any single month.
Increase profit per order by improving price, ad efficiency and listing conversion, not just by adding sales volume.
Watch PPC as a controllable line you can cut back when unit economics are thin.
caveats: The card's numbers are one seller's illustrative months, not benchmarks — your category fee percentage, FBA size tier and ad costs will differ.
The source's arithmetic should be treated as illustrative; always recalculate from your own invoices.

cards.title: Use Amazon keywords as demand research
cards.summary: Treat Amazon as a search engine: find keywords with meaningful search volume and low competition to pick a product people are already searching to buy.
cards.use_when: Product selection for private label or a new category, before committing inventory spend.
steps: Pick a niche or category first — the walkthrough stayed inside the pet/dog niche where he already had a brand.
Use a keyword research tool to measure how many shoppers search a phrase and how competitive the results are. The example found strong search demand for 'hands-free leash' with low competition.
Choose a product idea where search demand exists and rival listings are not saturated; this is the mechanism behind 'high demand, low competition'.
Use the same keyword data later for listing titles, backend terms and PPC targeting so research effort carries into launch.
Recheck demand before reordering, since search volumes and competitor counts shift.
caveats: The walkthrough's claim about search demand and competition is the presenter's method, not a guarantee of sales.
Tool metrics are estimates; verify against actual listing review counts and bestseller rank trends.

cards.title: Launch one SKU, not four colours
cards.summary: Splitting a first order across colour variants multiplies listings, packaging and inventory risk; launch a single SKU with all effort behind it.
cards.use_when: Deciding variant strategy and initial order composition for a private-label launch or first bundle line.
steps: Choose one SKU for launch: all spend and listing optimisation go behind a single ASIN instead of being divided.
Understand the arithmetic from the walkthrough: 200 units spread as 50 per colour meant four listings to write and manage and only 50 units of depth per variant, so popular colours sold out fast.
Concentrate inventory depth in the winning design; validate demand first, then add variants once you know which sells.
Keep packaging and prep simpler with one configuration — this is one of the largest hidden costs of variants, alongside the fourfold listing work.
If you do need multiple barcodes, buy them in the correct quantity (four UPCs cost ~$120 in the walkthrough) and only after demand is proven.
caveats: Variant strategy can be legitimate for some categories; the source's advice is specifically about a cash-constrained first launch.
The '$2,500 cost' figure is the presenter's own cost attribution, not a general penalty for variants.

cards.title: Plan for success: avoid stockouts
cards.summary: Running out of inventory during a ramp loses ranking and bestseller status; hold excess or reorder early enough to survive a good launch and seasonal peaks.
cards.use_when: Order sizing and replenishment planning around launch and peak seasons such as Christmas.
steps: Assume launches can go better than expected: the walkthrough sold out in month two because only the minimum order was placed out of fear after a prior failure.
Budget for a reorder before the first order sells through, not after it sells out — the presenter describes fixing this by reinvesting proceeds and leveraging other capital.
Recognise the ranking cost: a stockout caused loss of the 'new bestseller' badge and a visible sales drop equal to the earlier launch gains.
For seasonal operations, expect volume multiples around Christmas — the source reports triple volume, so plan peak inventory well ahead. Treat the multiple as the source's own seasonal experience.
As stock velocity becomes visible, automate min/max pricing so a high-velocity SKU keeps converting while you wait for the reorder to arrive.
Balance against over-ordering: the same walkthrough shows a loss month when sales did not cover expenses, so size reorders on observed velocity, not optimism alone.
caveats: There is no universal safety-stock formula in the source; the guidance is to hold cushion proportional to observed demand and lead time.
Stockpiling ties up cash and risks dead inventory if demand was temporary.

cards.title: Sell a differentiated passion product, not generic private label
cards.summary: Generic private-label items blend in and stall even with good PPC; a differentiated product can sustain momentum and extend to your own site and other channels.
cards.use_when: Choosing what to build a brand around, and deciding whether to keep pushing a me-too product or pivot.
steps: Diagnose the failure pattern first: the walkthrough's leash product was well designed and advertised but declined after month seven because nothing made it stand out from competitors.
Weigh differentiation as a strategy, not just a design choice — the more unique the product, the less you compete purely on price and the Box holders' terms.
Choose a product you have genuine interest in, which the source argues makes sustained marketing and a brand voice more achievable.
Look ahead to channels: a unique product can also be sold on your own website, Etsy and to retail or wholesale buyers, adding revenue beyond Amazon's fee stack.

Expect to invest more in product development and to learn faster via structured training than by trial-and-error alone; the walkthrough argues course-based learning compressed two years of garage time into months.
caveats: 'Passion product' is the presenter's positioning, and the income figures quoted are personal/team results rather than typical outcomes.
Products and niches differ — generic private label can work in some categories, and the source's own example shows it declined there.

cards.title: Launch quickly once the product is ready
cards.summary: Delaying a finished product ties up cash and loses the recurring monthly profit it could have produced; get to launch in months, not years.
cards.use_when: Deciding whether to shortcut research paralysis, outsource help, or take a course when a finished product is sitting unlaunched.
steps: Treat time-to-launch as a cost: the case study had a product sitting for two years, which the seller frames as thousands of dollars per month forfeited.
Set a target launch window rather than an open-ended perfection timeline; the source cites 3-6 months with support versus two years solo.
Decide deliberately whether to invest in training or help. The source's argument is that paid instruction compresses the learning curve and can be cheaper than two years of delay.
Do not interpret speed as skipping the profit math — the presenter's own costly mistake was ordering inventory without calculating expected profit, so speed and rigour go together.

Use launch-ready assets in parallel: packaging design took under two weeks in the walkthrough (one week of design plus revisions), so the critical path is often sourcing lead time and inventory depth, not creative.
caveats: Advice to buy a course is the presenter's commercial interest; weigh training cost against your own learning speed and the delay cost.
Rushing launch without unit-economic checks creates the opposite failure — the source's own costly mistake was ordering inventory before doing the math.
